before.exam_tip_html: On the 15-mark “Discuss” question, examiners want you to present multiple views with reasons — not just describe one side. On marriage and sexuality, that means: at minimum, a traditional religious view and a progressive or non-religious view, with reasons for each. Always name your religious tradition (Christianity or Islam) and use specific teachings or texts where you can. The command word “Discuss” requires a justified conclusion — you must say which view you find most persuasive and why. SPaG is assessed here, so spell key terms accurately: “fidelity,” “cohabitation,” “celibacy,” “contraception,” “procreation.” For shorter “Explain” questions (6 marks), two well-developed points each supported by a teaching or source of authority will reach the top band.

The 15-mark Discuss questions on this topic often ask whether one marga is more important than others, or whether selfless action or devotion is the best path to moksha. When you Discuss, present both sides: for example, jnana yoga proponents argue that wisdom directly removes the ignorance causing samsara, while bhakti traditions (especially Ramanuja) counter that love for God is the highest form of realisation. Name specific sources — Bhagavad Gita II 47 for karma yoga, IX 26–28 for bhakti yoga — to access the top mark band. A common student error is treating the four margas as mutually exclusive; examiners reward candidates who show that Hinduism allows — even encourages — following more than one simultaneously. Check the spelling of technical terms: varnashramadharma, svadharma, moksha and nishkam karma are all assessed in SPaG on the extended response.

For the 15-mark “Discuss” on pacifism, you need to present both absolute and conditional pacifist positions, not just argue one side. Name specific individuals (Gandhi, Martin Luther King, Desmond Tutu, Quaker Declaration 1660) and specific teachings (Matthew 5:38–42, Matthew 5:43–44). The most common error is treating all pacifists as holding the same view — examiners want to see you distinguish absolute from conditional pacifism. Spell “pacifism” and “non-violence” correctly; SPaG is assessed on your extended response.

The predestination topic (al-Qadr) is one of the most nuanced in this unit. Examiners reward students who go beyond simply saying “Muslims believe in fate” and instead explain the Mu’tazilite vs Al-Ash’ari debate, or the tension between divine foreknowledge and human freedom. For Barzakh, make sure you can distinguish it clearly from both death itself and from the final afterlife state — it is the ‘in between.’ For a 15-mark Discuss question on life after death, argue both that literal interpretations reinforce moral seriousness and that metaphorical interpretations may better capture the ineffable nature of the divine. Cite Surah 2:155 (testing), Surah 33:38 (destiny), Surah 101 (Day of Judgement). SPaG marks reward correct spelling: ‘al-Qadr’, ‘Akhirah’, ‘Barzakh’, ‘Jahannam’, ‘Mu’tazilite’.
